facts: charge-on-the-electron
The charge on an oil droplet is always an integral multiple of the electronic charge: q = n e
Millikan measured the effect of field strength on droplet motion to establish this
charge-on-the-electron
In Millikan's chamber three forces act on the drop: gravitational, electrostatic, and viscous drag while moving
thomson-model
Thomson proposed in 1898 that the atom is a sphere of radius about 10⁻¹⁰ m with positive charge distributed uniformly
Electrons are embedded in it so the atom is electrically neutral
fundamental-particles
The electron carries −1.602176×10⁻¹⁹ C and has mass 9.109382×10⁻³¹ kg
Relative charge −1; mass about 0.00054 u
fundamental-particles
The proton carries +1.602176×10⁻¹⁹ C with mass 1.6726216×10⁻²⁷ kg; the neutron is uncharged with mass 1.674927×10⁻²⁷ kg
rutherford-scattering
High energy α-particles were directed at a gold foil about 100 nm thick surrounded by a fluorescent zinc sulphide screen
rutherford-scattering
Most α-particles passed through the foil undeflected; a small fraction were deflected
Only a very small number were deflected through large angles
rutherford-scattering
The deflections showed the positive charge is concentrated in a very small volume, not spread through the atom as Thomson supposed
An enormous repulsive force is needed to turn an α-particle back
nuclear-model
If a nucleus were the size of a cricket ball, the atom's radius would be about 5 km
atomic-and-mass-number
Atomic number Z equals the number of protons in the nucleus and the number of electrons in a neutral atom
atomic-and-mass-number
A species is written with mass number A as a left superscript and atomic number Z as a left subscript on the symbol
isotopes-and-isobars
99.985% of hydrogen atoms contain only one proton; this isotope is protium
The remainder are deuterium and tritium
isotopes-and-isobars
Chemical properties of atoms are controlled by the number of electrons, determined by the proton count
The number of neutrons has very little effect on chemical properties
drawbacks-of-rutherford-model
An electron in a planet-like orbit is under acceleration even at constant speed, because its direction changes
Classical electromagnetic theory then requires it to radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus
drawbacks-of-rutherford-model
The Rutherford model cannot explain the stability of an atom
The predicted collapse does not happen
electromagnetic-radiation
The oscillating electric and magnetic fields are perpendicular to each other and both perpendicular to the direction of propagation
electromagnetic-radiation
Frequency, wavelength and the speed of light are related by c = ν λ
electromagnetic-radiation
Wavenumber is the number of wavelengths per unit length, with units of reciprocal length
heisenberg-uncertainty
For milligram-sized or heavier objects the uncertainty in position and velocity is insignificant
The product ∆v∆x obtained is extremely small
heisenberg-uncertainty
An orbit is a clearly defined path, which requires knowing position and velocity exactly at the same time
The uncertainty principle forbids this, so the idea of an orbit fails for an electron
quantum-mechanical-model
Quantised energy states and their wave functions are characterised by three quantum numbers: n, l and ml
They arise as a natural consequence of the quantum mechanical treatment
quantum-mechanical-model
The wave function's value depends on the electron's coordinates and by itself carries no physical meaning
quantum-mechanical-model
An atomic orbital is the wave function ψ for an electron in an atom
An electron described by a wave function is said to occupy that orbital
quantum-mechanical-model
For hydrogen and hydrogen-like species the energy and size of an orbital depend only on n
In multi-electron atoms the energies depend on more than n alone
probability-density
The probability of finding an electron at a point is proportional to |ψ|², the probability density, which is always positive
probability-density
For a 2s orbital the probability density falls sharply to zero, rises again to a small maximum, then decreases towards zero
The 1s orbital does not show this intermediate zero
principal-quantum-number
The principal quantum number identifies the shell, and orbital energy increases as n increases
Energy is required to move a negatively charged electron away from the nucleus
azimuthal-quantum-number
The number of subshells in a principal shell equals the value of n
For n = 2 the possible l values are 0 and 1; for n = 3 they are 0, 1 and 2
azimuthal-quantum-number
l values 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 correspond to the subshell notations s, p, d, f, g, h
magnetic-quantum-number
For l = 2 the magnetic quantum number takes five values, −2 to +2, giving five d orbitals
The count is 2l+1
magnetic-quantum-number
For a given l, ml has (2l+1) values, which is the number of orbitals in that subshell
magnetic-quantum-number
The values of ml are derived from l, and the values of l are derived from n
spin-quantum-number
The three quantum numbers n, l and ml are not enough to explain the doublets and triplets seen in multi-electron line spectra
spin-quantum-number
An electron has intrinsic spin angular momentum, a vector with two possible orientations relative to a chosen axis
orbit-versus-orbital
Orbit and orbital are not synonymous
An orbit as proposed by Bohr is a circular path around the nucleus
orbit-versus-orbital
An orbital is characterised by three quantum numbers n, l and ml, and its value depends on the electron's coordinates
ψ itself has no physical meaning; |ψ|² does
orbit-versus-orbital
An orbital described by n = 2, l = 1, ml = 0 is a p orbital of the second shell
Each orbital is defined by a set of values for n, l and ml

methods.name: Counting protons, neutrons and electrons from A(Z)X
methods.trigger: A species written with mass number and atomic number, asked for particle counts
steps: Check first whether the species is a neutral atom, a cation or an anion
Electrons = Z for a neutral atom; adjust by the charge for an ion
methods.common_error: Applying electrons = Z to a charged species; the notation looks identical for ions

methods.name: Enumerating orbitals from the quantum numbers
methods.trigger: A shell or subshell given, asked how many orbitals or which quantum numbers are allowed
steps: From n, list allowed l as 0 to n−1
For each l, ml runs −l to +l, giving 2l+1 orbitals
Sum across subshells for the shell total
methods.common_error: Deriving l from ml rather than the other way round — l comes from n, and ml from l

methods.name: Converting wavelength, frequency and wavenumber
methods.trigger: A radiation given in one unit, asked for another
steps: Convert the given wavelength to metres
Use c = ν λ for frequency
Use wavenumber = 1/λ, watching whether cm⁻¹ or m⁻¹ is wanted
Check the answer sits in the expected region of the spectrum
methods.common_error: Mixing cm and m when computing wavenumber, which shifts the answer by a factor of 100

connections: An orbit needs exact position and velocity at once, which the uncertainty principle forbids — this is why an electron has an orbital, not an orbit.
The classical prediction that an orbiting electron must radiate and collapse is what forced a quantum treatment.
The wave function has no physical meaning by itself; |ψ|² is what can be interpreted, as probability density.
l fixes how many orientations are possible: ml takes 2l+1 values.
For a shell of principal quantum number n there are exactly n subshells, l running 0 to n−1.
The large-angle deflections are the evidence that the positive charge sits in a tiny dense nucleus.
Isotopes share Z and differ in A; isobars share A and differ in Z.
misconceptions: An orbital is the path the electron travels around the nucleus
The Bohr picture of a circular path is taught first and is easier to draw, so the word orbital gets read as a tidier orbit
The electron is somewhere on the surface of the orbital
Boundary surface diagrams look like shells, which suggests the electron sits on them rather than anywhere within the region
The wave function ψ itself tells you where the electron is
ψ is what gets written down and plotted, so it looks like the meaningful quantity; it is |ψ|² that has physical meaning
In every atom the energy of an orbital depends only on n
It is true for hydrogen and hydrogen-like species, which is where it is first taught, but not for multi-electron atoms
Isotopes of an element differ in chemical properties because they have different masses
Mass differences are real and measurable, but chemistry is controlled by electrons, and isotopes have the same electron count
The value of l is chosen independently of n
Each quantum number is introduced as a separate rule, which hides that l is derived from n and ml from l
